Learning New Songs; Series 1 HEAR IT BEFORE YOU SING IT A new song arrives. You listen once, twice, perhaps several times, and soon you feel familiar with it. But familiarity is not the same as knowing the song. Can you sing the melody without the recording? Can you find it on your instrument? Can you identify where the verse ends and the chorus begins? Can you recognise a chord change or anticipate your entrance? This is where real learning begins: with your ears. Learning by ear is one of the most valuable skills a singer or musician can develop. It teaches you to listen carefully, identify what you hear, and reproduce it accurately. Written music, lyrics, chord charts and tutorials are valuable tools, but your ears should not always depend on your eyes. Listen to the Whole Song First Before trying to sing or play anything, listen to the complete song. Pay attention to: The melody Rhythm and tempo Song structure Bass movement Chords and harmony Dynamics Instrumentation Emotional character Then choose a small section to work on. The “Listen–Pause–Reproduce” Method Don’t start by attacking the entire song. Listen → Pause → Reproduce → Check → Repeat For a singer, listen to a short phrase, pause the recording and sing it back. For an instrumentalist, listen to the phrase, identify the starting note and work out the melody on your instrument. For a choir, learn your section’s part in short phrases before attempting the entire arrangement. This method trains your ears instead of making you dependent on continuous playback. From my experience working with singers, instrumentalists and choirs, I have noticed that performers with stronger listening skills become more independent. They begin to recognise patterns, anticipate musical changes and respond more confidently when something unexpected happens. PRACTICE PLAN — 20 MINUTES Listen to the whole song – 5 minutes. Identify the structure and difficult sections – 5 minutes. Learn one short phrase by ear – 5 minutes. Reproduce it without the recording – 5 minutes Today’s goal: Don’t finish the song. Learn one section accurately. “Before you ask your voice or instrument to reproduce the music, train your ears to understand what the music is saying.”— Victor Adenola Once your ears can capture the music, the next step is turning what you hear into reliable musical memory. #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #music #musicDirector #musicians #musicperformance #practicing #rehearsal #rehearsals #singer #singers #songStructure
